resources.string: Estimated by Ayuvo from your own data using published formulas. It is not a medical measurement or diagnosis; talk to your doctor about anything that concerns you.

Your lowest steady heart rate while asleep, estimated from minute-by-minute heart rate when your device does not provide a resting heart rate.
Average heart rate across last night\'s main sleep.
The single lowest heart-rate reading during last night\'s sleep.
How much lower your heart rate is asleep than awake. A dip of 10% or more is the usual healthy pattern.
Your heart rate while sitting still during the day (09:00-21:00), when you took no steps for at least 10 minutes.
Average, lowest and highest heart rate while awake today.
Highest heart rate held for at least 2 minutes today.
Your estimated maximum heart rate, used to set heart-rate zones.
The gap between your maximum and resting heart rate. A larger reserve usually means better fitness.
Minutes your heart rate was in the moderate or vigorous range, with vigorous minutes counted twice. WHO recommends 150-300 a week.
A load score that weighs time by how hard your heart worked. Harder minutes count exponentially more.
An estimate of your VO₂max from your maximum and resting heart rate. It is a rough guide; an outdoor GPS workout gives a better estimate.
How far today\'s resting heart rate is from your 30-day average. Two days in a row 5 bpm or more above usual can mean strain, poor sleep or getting ill.
How many minutes today your wearable recorded heart rate. A day with 10 hours or more is counted as a valid day.
Your average heart rate while walking. It usually falls as fitness improves.
Share of your time in bed spent asleep. 85% or more is considered good.
How long it took to fall asleep after getting into bed. Up to 30 minutes is typical.
Share of sleep spent in deep sleep. Adults usually spend about 13-23%.
Share of sleep spent in REM. Adults usually spend about 20-25%.
Times you were awake for 5 minutes or more after first falling asleep.
Halfway between falling asleep and waking. It tracks your body-clock timing.
Minutes from falling asleep to the first deep sleep.
Minutes from falling asleep to the first REM sleep. Typically 70-120 minutes.
How much your bedtime varies across the last 14 nights. Under 30-60 minutes is regular.
The chance you are in the same state (asleep or awake) at the same time on consecutive days, scaled to 100. Higher is more regular.
How much later you sleep on weekends than on weekdays. Under 1 hour is best.
Your natural body-clock timing: the midpoint of sleep on free days, corrected for catching up on sleep.
Sleep you missed against your nightly need over the last 14 nights. Adults need at least 7 hours.
Minutes you walked at 100 steps a minute or faster, which counts as moderate activity.
The average of your 30 fastest minutes of stepping today.
Hours between 07:00 and 22:00 with at least 250 steps. Breaking up sitting every hour is recommended.
Your longest run of minutes without a step between 07:00 and 22:00 while wearing your device.
Your daily steps placed in the Tudor-Locke bands: sedentary <5,000, low active 5,000-7,499, somewhat active 7,500-9,999, active 10,000-12,499, highly active ≥12,500.
Steps your wearable counted while your phone counted almost none, for example when the phone stayed at home.
Consecutive days you reached your step goal.
Average step length from your phone\'s distance and steps, compared with the typical length for your height.
All the energy your body used today: resting, activity and digesting food.
Energy used at rest per day from your device, next to the Mifflin-St Jeor prediction.
Total energy burned ÷ resting energy. 1.40-1.69 is sedentary to lightly active, 1.70-1.99 active, 2.00-2.40 vigorously active.
Your typical walking speed over the last 7 days. Below 0.8 m/s is linked with higher health risk in older adults.
Share of each step with both feet on the ground. Typical values are 20-40%; higher can mean less balance.
Walking readings in the last 7 days where one step was more than 10% different from the other.
How much of the weekly safe-listening allowance you used, where 100% a week is 80 dB for 40 hours.
Your weight with day-to-day water swings smoothed out.
How fast your smoothed weight is changing per week.
Body mass index from your smoothed weight and height.
The weight range with a healthy BMI for your height.
How many weeks until you reach your goal weight at your current rate.
Protein you logged per kilogram of body weight. 1.4-2.0 g/kg a day supports strength training.
Share of your energy from protein, carbohydrate and fat, from the grams you logged.
Share of your energy from saturated fat. WHO recommends below 10%.
Fibre per 1,000 kcal you ate. About 14 g per 1,000 kcal is recommended.
Molar ratio of sodium to potassium. WHO suggests keeping it below 1. Salt added while cooking is often not in food estimates.
Time from your first to your last logged food, using the time you ate it.
Time between your last food and going to bed.
Times you had tea or coffee within an hour of an iron-rich food, which can reduce how much iron you absorb.
Calories you logged minus the energy you burned today.
What your body likely burns per day, worked out from what you ate and how your weight trend changed over 4 weeks.
Lowest average of 5 consecutive minutes inside last night\'s main sleep. Needs at least 3 hours of sleep with heart rate on at least 70% of those minutes.
Mean of every heart-rate minute inside the main sleep window.
Minimum heart-rate minute inside the main sleep window.
1 − (sleeping average ÷ awake average over the 14 hours after waking) × 100. Needs at least 4 hours of awake heart rate.
Mean of daytime heart-rate minutes where the current and previous 10 minutes had no steps. Needs 30 such minutes.
Mean, minimum and maximum of heart-rate minutes outside the main sleep window. Needs 60 minutes.
Maximum of 2-minute rolling averages, which ignores single-reading spikes.
Tanaka formula 208 − 0.7 × age, raised to the highest 2-minute heart rate seen in the last 180 days when that is higher.
Maximum heart rate − resting heart rate (Karvonen).

Each heart-rate minute is classed by % heart-rate reserve (moderate 40-59%, vigorous 60-89%, near-maximal ≥90%). Without a resting heart rate % of maximum is used (moderate 64-76%, vigorous 77-95%, near-maximal ≥96%). Moderate + 2 × (vigorous + near-maximal).
Banister TRIMP over minutes at ≥30% heart-rate reserve: Σ minutes × HRr × 0.64 × e^(k × HRr), k = 1.92 for men and 1.67 for women.
Uth-Sørensen: 15.3 × maximum heart rate ÷ resting heart rate. Low confidence when the maximum comes from the age formula.
Today − mean of the previous 30 days (needs 14 days). Flag when today and yesterday are both at least 5 bpm above.
Count of minutes with a heart-rate reading in the local day.
Mean heart rate in minutes with 60-130 steps, in runs of 3 or more such minutes (faster minutes count as running). Needs 10 minutes.
First asleep stage − start of time in bed. Needs an In Bed record.
Deep minutes ÷ time asleep × 100. Only nights with sleep stages.
REM minutes ÷ time asleep × 100. Only nights with sleep stages.
Gaps of ≥5 minutes between asleep stages, from first sleep to final waking. Minutes awake are shown as wake after sleep onset.
Start of the first sleep record, as a clock time.
End of the last asleep stage, as a clock time.
Sleep onset + half the time to final waking.
Sample standard deviation of bedtime (and wake time) over the last 14 nights. Needs 5 nights.
Minute-by-minute comparison of each noon-to-noon day with the next over the last 14 days: 200 × agreement − 100. Needs 5 day pairs.
|Mean sleep midpoint on free nights (waking Saturday or Sunday) − on work nights|. Needs 2 free and 3 work nights in 14 days.
MSFsc = MSF − (SDf − SDweek) ÷ 2 when free-day sleep is longer than weekday sleep, where SDweek = (5 × SDw + 2 × SDf) ÷ 7.
Σ max(0, need − time asleep) over recorded nights in the last 14 days. Need defaults to 8 hours.
Minutes with ≥100 steps from your wearable\'s minute data.
Mean of the 30 highest minute step counts in the day.
Count of hours 07:00-21:59 whose de-duplicated steps are ≥250.
Longest run of worn minutes (heart rate present) with no steps, 07:00-21:59.
Band of the day\'s de-duplicated step total.
Flagged when the wearable counts ≥1,000 steps and the phone less than 10% of that.
Days in a row meeting the goal, counting today once it is met.
Distance ÷ steps from the same source (needs 1,000 steps). Typical = 0.415 × height for men and 0.413 × height for women.
(Resting + active energy) ÷ 0.9, adding about 10% for digestion. Needs a full day of resting energy (at least 70% of your predicted BMR).
Daily resting energy; prediction 10 × kg + 6.25 × cm − 5 × age + 5 (men) or − 161 (women).
Median of walking-speed readings in the last 7 days.
Median of double-support readings in the last 7 days.
Count of asymmetry readings >10% (readings of 100% are treated as sensor errors). Flagged at 3 or more.
Exponentially smoothed average: trend += 0.1 × (weigh-in − trend) on each day with a weigh-in.
(Trend today − trend 14 days ago) ÷ 2. Needs 4 weigh-ins in 14 days.
Trend weight ÷ height². WHO categories, or the Asian cut-offs (overweight ≥23, obese ≥27.5) if chosen in Settings.
18.5 × height² to 24.9 × height² (22.9 with Asian cut-offs).
(Goal − trend) ÷ weekly rate, when moving towards the goal at ≥0.05 kg a week.
4 kcal/g protein and carbohydrate, 9 kcal/g fat; each share of their total.
9 × saturated fat g ÷ energy from macros × 100.
Last eaten time − first eaten time.
Count of tea/coffee items within 60 minutes of an item with ≥3 mg iron.
Mean logged kcal − (trend change × 7,700 kcal/kg) ÷ 28 days. Needs 14 logged days and 6 weigh-ins.

AI explanations describe these numbers. They are not medical advice.
Your phone decides when background refresh runs, so a morning score can appear later than you expect.
Wellness estimates from your own data, not a medical diagnosis or advice.
Ayuvo Health Age is Ayuvo\'s own estimate from your data. It is not a clinical or biological age, and it is not WHOOP\'s or any other company\'s score.
An association in your data, not proof of cause.
How Ayuvo Health Age is estimated
When there is not enough data
Scores are calculated from your synced health data each time you open them, so there is no separate score history to keep in sync.
Ayuvo asks your phone to refresh Recovery in the morning after sleep syncs. iOS and Android decide when background work actually runs, so it may appear later, or only when you open the app.
The optional Recovery and Daily Review notifications only say that something is ready. They never show your values.
Ayuvo compares each reading with your own recent history, not with other people. Your baseline for a metric is the average of the previous 60 days, not counting today.

A baseline needs at least 14 days with a reading. Until then you will see \"Learning your baseline\" with a count such as 9/14. Confidence is high when at least 70% of the 60 days have data and there are 30 or more readings, and medium otherwise.

Your normal range is your average plus or minus one standard deviation, the usual spread of your readings. A minimum spread is used for each metric, so a very steady history does not make tiny changes look dramatic.
Ayuvo shows the difference from your average, the percentage change and how many spreads away today is. Trends use the slope of the last 28 days, shown as a percentage of your baseline per week.

HRV, resting heart rate, blood oxygen and breathing rate use readings taken during last night\'s sleep. When no reading falls inside your sleep window, the daily value is used instead and marked as such.
Baselines depend on how often you wear your device and on its sensors. A missing reading is shown as missing, never as zero.
A look back at one day: a Day Score from 0 to 100, what went well, what needs attention, what to try tomorrow and what to consider reducing.

Nutrition 30%, activity 20%, sleep 20%, hydration 10%, training 10%, recovery 10% and fasting 10%. Only areas you track and have data for count, and the weights are scaled to what is included. An area you did not log shows as not logged and never lowers your score.

Nutrition: calories within 10% of your target, protein at 90% or more of your target, fiber at your goal and carbs and fat within 20% of target. Hydration and steps: progress toward your goals. Training: a workout, or a rest day after a hard day. Sleep: last night compared with 7 hours. Recovery: this morning\'s score.
Nutrients with an upper limit you set, such as sugar, sodium, saturated fat or caffeine, are compared with that limit and your 28-day average. Patterns from your own data can appear here too.
The review can only see what was logged or synced. It describes your day; it is not medical advice.

Ayuvo Health Age is Ayuvo\'s own estimate of how your recent habits and fitness markers compare with published population values. It is not a clinical or biological age, and it is not WHOOP\'s or any other company\'s score.
VO2 max 25%, resting heart rate 15%, heart rate variability 15%, daily steps 15%, sleep 15%, workout consistency 10% and body composition 5%. Each marker uses your average over the last 90 days.

VO2 max and HRV are compared with population averages by age and sex: the age at which the average equals your value, minus your actual age. Resting heart rate, steps, sleep, workouts and body composition use tables that turn each range into a number of years. Each marker is limited to 6 years either way (3 for HRV), and the total to 10.
Your birthday in your profile, and at least 3 markers including VO2 max, resting heart rate or HRV. Most markers need 30 days of data in the last 90; VO2 max needs 3 readings and body composition 1.

Health Age is recalculated for each of the last 12 weeks. Pace is how fast it has been changing per calendar year: below 0.9 is improving, 0.9 to 1.1 is steady and above 1.1 is rising faster than time. Pace needs at least 8 weekly points.

Population tables come from specific groups and lab methods, and watch readings are estimates. HRV norms come from resting ECG recordings, so that marker is kept small. Treat the number as a direction to watch, not a verdict.
Ayuvo compares days with and without something, such as a late intense workout, and looks at what happened next, such as that night\'s sleep.

Over the last 120 days, each group needs at least 8 days. Ayuvo compares the two averages with Welch\'s t test and an effect size (Cohen\'s d). A pattern is shown only when the difference is both consistent (t of 2 or more) and large enough to matter (d of 0.3 or more).

Late intense workouts and that night\'s sleep; high training load and next-day recovery; meeting your water goal and next-day recovery; meeting your protein target and next-day strength volume; a short night and that day\'s steps.
An association in your data, not proof of cause. Other things that happen on the same days can explain a difference.
Recovery is a 0-100 morning score that compares last night\'s body signals with your own baselines. It is ready once last night\'s sleep has synced.

Heart rate variability counts for 35%, resting heart rate 25%, sleep 25%, breathing rate 7.5% and blood oxygen 7.5%. Sleep is 70% duration compared with your usual and 30% how close your sleep midpoint was to the previous 14 nights. Missing inputs are left out and the remaining weights are scaled up.

Each input starts at 50 for a typical night and moves 20 points for each spread above or below your usual, in the healthy direction: higher HRV scores higher, a higher resting heart rate scores lower. Breathing rate only lowers the score when it is well outside your usual range, and blood oxygen only when it is well below your usual.
When yesterday\'s training load was high compared with your 28-day average, 3 points are taken off, or 6 when it was more than double the average.
67 and above is Good Recovery (normal training), 34 to 66 is Moderate (consider lighter training) and below 34 is Low (a recovery-focused day).
Recovery needs a sleep baseline and an HRV or resting heart rate baseline, each with at least 14 nights. Nights with less than 2 hours of recorded sleep are treated as incomplete.
Illness, alcohol, travel, stress and device fit can all move these signals. Recovery is a wellness estimate from your own data, not a medical diagnosis or advice.
On days with late intense workouts, your sleep that night has been {abs_diff} {unit} {direction_word} on average ({n_exposed} vs {n_unexposed} days).
After high training-load days, your next-day recovery has been {abs_diff} {unit} {direction_word} on average ({n_exposed} vs {n_unexposed} days).
After days you met your water goal, your next-day recovery has been {abs_diff} {unit} {direction_word} on average ({n_exposed} vs {n_unexposed} days).
After days you met your protein target, your next-day strength volume has been {abs_diff} {unit} {direction_word} on average ({n_exposed} vs {n_unexposed} days).
On days after a short night, you have taken {abs_diff} {direction_word} {unit} on average ({n_exposed} vs {n_unexposed} days).
